title: Modesty brings good
hookLine: a man scolds his brother for being too shy, and the Prophet steps in

cards: A man of the Ansar is lecturing his brother: you're too shy. You hold back too much. It's costing you.
It's the kind of advice people still give. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, was passing by and heard it. In Sahih al-Bukhari, in paraphrase, he said: leave him.
Haya' is part of faith. He didn't side with the confident brother. He defended the shy one.

teach.b: Haya' is hard to put into one English word: modesty, shyness, a sense of shame in the good sense, the inner brake that stops a hand before it does something low.
The hadith of the day is from 'Imran ibn Husayn, in Bukhari, in paraphrase: haya' brings nothing but good.
Not mostly good. Only good. It isn't timidity, the fear that keeps someone from speaking a truth.
It's closer to conscience with a blush.
Abu Sa'id describes the Prophet himself, in Bukhari, in paraphrase: he was more shy than a young girl behind her curtain, and when he disliked something, you could see it in his face.

teach.h: NO HAYA'? DO WHAT YOU LIKE.
teach.b: Then Bukhari keeps a saying the Prophet traced to the words of the first prophecy, in paraphrase: if you have no haya', do whatever you like. It reads like permission, but it's a warning.
Without that inner brake, nothing stops anything. Haya' is the pause before the cruel comment, the post that shows off, the glance that takes too much.
Tradition speaks of it facing two ways: haya' before people, and haya' before Allah, the sense of being seen even when the room is empty. Both make a person a little slower to do what they'd regret.
That's why it brings only good.

how: In Islamic teaching, haya', modesty and shyness before people and before Allah, is part of faith, drawing on hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari that say haya' brings nothing but good.

o: the shyness that keeps you from ever speaking up for truth
a modest inner brake that keeps you from doing what's low
the shame you feel after you've already done wrong

p: leave him; haya' is part of faith
his dislike showed in his face

s: the Prophet told the shy man to be more confident
he told the brother: leave him, haya' is part of faith.
the hadith says haya' brings nothing but good
'if you have no haya', do whatever you like' is a permission
it's a warning: without the inner brake, nothing stops anything.

games.q: passing by, the Prophet hears a man scolding his brother for being too shy. what does he say?
o: he's right; shyness holds people back.
leave him; haya' is part of faith.
games.why: he defended the shy brother: leave him, for haya' is part of faith (Bukhari).

practice: Run back through yesterday and look for a moment where a small pause might have helped: a joke one step too far, a story told mostly to look good, something shared that didn't need sharing.
Don't judge it; just find the spot where the brake could have touched, and choose one place today to let haya' work, speaking a little less about yourself or letting someone's mistake go unmentioned.
If you pray, you can ask for haya'.

wordCard.voice: Haya'. Modesty and shyness, an inner brake before people and before Allah, that the hadith says brings nothing but good. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: modesty, shyness, an inner brake.

carryVoice: Your line: only good. Not mostly good, but only good. Tomorrow, truthfulness and the company it keeps.
